title: Interfaces & Object Shapes
description: Model data structures with interfaces — the backbone of typed configs, API responses, and domain objects.

challenges.title: What is an interface?
challenges.description:
What does a TypeScript interface define?

  A)  A class that can be instantiated
  B)  The shape of an object — what properties and types it must have
  C)  A runtime value that validates objects
  D)  A function signature only
challenges.whyMatters: Every config object, API response, and environment manifest you work with has a shape — interfaces let you express that shape and catch mismatches at compile time.

choices.label: A)  A class that can be instantiated
B)  The shape of an object — what properties and types it must have
C)  A runtime value that validates objects

challenges.title: Interface vs type alias
challenges.description:
Which of these is valid syntax for both an interface AND a type alias?

  A)  Describing the shape of an object
  B)  Extending another type with &
  C)  Declaring a union like string | number
  D)  Using implements in a class
challenges.whyMatters: You'll see both in real codebases — knowing the difference prevents confusion when reading infrastructure code written by others.
hints: type aliases can express unions, interfaces cannot directly

choices.label: A)  Describing the shape of an object
C)  Declaring a union like string | number
D)  Using implements in a class

challenges.title: Optional properties
challenges.description:
In this interface, which property is optional?

  interface ServiceConfig {
    host: string
    port: number
    timeout?: number
  }

And what type does `timeout` have inside the object when accessed?
challenges.whyMatters: Optional config fields are everywhere — timeouts, retry counts, feature flags. Understanding optionality means you don't accidentally treat undefined as a number.
hints: The ? makes a property optional, which means its type becomes T | undefined

challenges.title: Write a ServiceConfig interface
challenges.description:
Write an interface `ServiceConfig` with:
- `host` (string, required)
- `port` (number, required)
- `timeout` (number, optional)
- `retries` (number, optional)

Then write a function `buildUrl` that accepts a `ServiceConfig` and returns a string like `http://localhost:8080` (ignore timeout/retries in the URL).
challenges.whyMatters: You'll write functions like this for health check endpoints, service discovery clients, and HTTP client wrappers.

challenges.title: Extending interfaces
challenges.whyMatters: Extending interfaces models inheritance in your domain — a DeployedService extends a Service which extends a Resource. Common in infrastructure typings.
hints: extends means the child must satisfy ALL properties of both interfaces

challenges.title: Model a deployment manifest
challenges.description:
Model a simplified deployment manifest using two interfaces:

`Resource` with: `id` (string), `name` (string), `labels` (Record<string, string>)

`Deployment` extending `Resource` with: `image` (string), `replicas` (number), `env` (Record<string, string>, optional)

Then write a function `describeDeployment` that accepts a `Deployment` and returns a string:
`"[id] name → image x replicas replicas"`

Example: `"[abc123] api-server → nginx:latest x 3 replicas"`
challenges.whyMatters: This is exactly the shape of a Kubernetes-style manifest. Typing these structures is day-one software engineering TypeScript work.
hints: Record<string, string> is a built-in utility type for string key/value maps
Use extends to build Deployment on top of Resource
